context: Topic: how vaccines train the immune system. You gave this speech to a nursing club. Now you will give it to a fifth-grade class.
prompt: Which adaptation fits the new audience best?

options.text: Keep the same slides; the science is the same.
options.feedback: The facts don't change, but the audience's knowledge does. Terms like "antigen" need translation or examples.

options.text: Use an analogy (a "wanted poster" that helps the body recognize a germ), define new words, and keep accuracy.
options.feedback: Yes. Analogies and definitions are supporting materials from Chapter 7. You simplify the language, not the truth.

options.text: Skip the science and tell a funny story instead.
options.feedback: Engagement matters, but the audience still deserves to learn the content.

context: You are asking members of a senior center to support a new skatepark near their building.
prompt: What is the most audience-centered first step?

options.text: Assume they will oppose it because they are older, and prepare to argue.
options.feedback: That is a stereotype. Age may suggest some shared experiences, but it doesn't tell you what any person thinks.

options.text: Ask a few members or the center director what concerns and hopes they have about the park.
options.feedback: Yes. The textbook emphasizes gathering real information. You may find shared values, such as safe places for grandchildren.

options.text: Speak louder and slower than normal for the whole speech.
options.feedback: Adjust volume for the room, not for assumptions about listeners.

context: At a family night, many parents speak languages other than English, and interpreters may be present.
prompt: Which adaptation is most respectful and effective?

options.text: Use plain language, avoid idioms, pause for interpreters, and show key information visually.
options.feedback: Yes. Clear language and visuals help everyone. Idioms ("hit it out of the park") often do not translate.

options.text: Talk more slowly and simplify the ideas because the audience may not understand complex topics.
options.feedback: Pacing can help, but simplifying the ideas assumes something about the audience's thinking. Language proficiency is not the same as understanding.

options.text: Keep it exactly as written; adapting would be unfair to English speakers.
options.feedback: Adaptations like clear language and visuals usually help all listeners.

context: Last year the school board voted down the same proposal you are presenting. Several members are still on the board.

options.text: Ignore last year's vote and present it as a brand-new idea.
options.feedback: The board remembers. Ignoring historical context can damage your credibility.

options.text: Acknowledge last year's concerns, explain what has changed, and start from shared goals.
options.feedback: Yes. Recognizing historical context and building common ground helps a skeptical audience listen.

options.text: Criticize last year's decision so they know you're serious.
options.feedback: Attacking the listeners you need to persuade makes them defensive.

context: Your speech will be delivered live on a video call to a class you cannot see well.
prompt: Which adaptation best addresses the online context?

options.text: Look at the camera when making key points, check lighting and audio beforehand, and build in moments for chat or questions.
options.feedback: Yes. Appendix C covers online preparation. The camera is your audience's eyes, and you need deliberate ways to get feedback.

options.text: Read from a script on screen since no one can tell.
options.feedback: Audiences often notice reading eyes, and you lose conversational delivery.

options.text: Turn off your camera so you feel less nervous.
options.feedback: Your nonverbal delivery is part of the message. Ask your instructor about camera expectations.
